correctness.rationale: The continuous-time law is a mixture of the product measures with coordinate means b and −b, where b=exp(−2t/n); the Poisson parity gives the weight difference h_t=exp(−2γ_n t). Walsh orthogonality gives the two binomial terms in the exact chi-square, with the odd levels multiplied by h_t². At the stated time b=a/√n and h_t→h also for θ=∞. The two log likelihoods under uniform measure have joint limit ±aZ−a²/2 (the Taylor remainder is O(n b³)); the exact second moments are bounded, so expectations of absolute deviations converge. Pairing z and −z gives the integral of max(|A(z)|,hB(z)) over positive z. The positive zero of A and B>0 around that zero yield strictness even when the smaller parameter is zero. Gaussian-integrable Taylor bounds give the two late coefficients, with E|Z²−1|=4φ(1). The finite-n law is sandwiched between its antipodal symmetrization and its pure-product endpoint in TV. The early symmetrized profile tends to 1 by applying bounded convergence to min(likelihood,1); the late product profile tends to 0. At each fixed c the two endpoint limits are strictly between 0 and 1, so the order-n scale is genuine even without convergence of the rates. The closing conclusions are for fixed parameters as stated, not a simultaneous limit h→0 and a→0.

value.rationale: A parity clock with a bounded expected number of flips on the mixing scale can change the entire limiting TV profile without moving the cutoff. The strict continuum, explicit asymptotic coefficients and uniform-in-rate cutoff distinguish two consequences of this natural perturbation that endpoint profiles or a spectral gap alone cannot quantify. The result is modest and elementary and claims neither new endpoints nor a general theorem for nonlocal walks.
